meta.purpose: Gulf trade name -> active ingredient(s). Used by Travel Check to turn a photographed box into something the interaction index can be keyed on.
meta.source: Saudi Food and Drug Authority public registered-drug list, https://www.sfda.gov.sa/en/drugs-list
meta.retrievedBy: filtered by Scientific Name in the SFDA public register; trade name, strength and dosage form copied verbatim from the returned row
meta.whySaudiDataForAKuwaitiApp: Kuwait and Saudi Arabia are both members of the GCC centralised drug registration framework (GCC-DR), under which a product registered centrally is marketed across member states under the same trade name. RxNorm and DrugBank are US-centric and do not carry Gulf trade names at all, so a US source cannot resolve a box bought in a Kuwaiti pharmacy. The SFDA register is free, public, requires no API key, and lists trade name alongside scientific name - which is exactly the mapping needed. It is a proxy, not an authority on the Kuwaiti market: a Kuwait-registered product absent from the Saudi register will not resolve, and under G2 that is a refusal, not a guess.
meta.scope: Deliberately small. Covers only the drugs used in the demo scenarios, as the project brief specifies. Widening it is a data task, not a code change.
meta.multiIngredientNote: A trade name may carry several active ingredients. Panadol Cold & Flu is paracetamol + pseudoephedrine + chlorpheniramine. Screening only the headline ingredient of a combination product would miss real interactions, so ingredients is always an array and Travel Check screens every member of it.

brands.ingredientNote: SFDA lists the scientific name as PARACETAMOL. DDInter indexes the same molecule as Acetaminophen. The mapping table is where that transatlantic naming split is resolved - which is precisely why a mapping layer has to exist rather than passing names straight through.
THE TRAVEL CHECK DEMO. One familiar box, three active ingredients. A patient abroad reads the front of the pack and thinks 'paracetamol'.
